strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem—training-free video reasoning segmentation—and demonstrates that MLLM attention maps can be repurposed for localization without any fine-tuning, which is a useful direction for the community.

The proposed Decomposed Attention Fusion (DecAF) is well-motivated and composed of two intuitive mechanisms: contrastive object–background fusion to suppress visual attention sinks, and complementary video–frame fusion to balance temporal context with object-centric spatial detail. The design choices are clearly explained and illustrated.

The evaluation is broad: three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL/2.5VL) and five datasets (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS), with both attention-only and SAM-based variants reported, giving good coverage of referring and reasoning VOS.

The ablation study is thorough and informative, isolating object–background fusion, video–frame fusion, multi-scale inputs, rollout normalization (V-Max), rollout starting layer, SAM prompting thresholds, and the attention consistency score. This helps justify each component of the pipeline.

The attention-guided SAM2 prompting with an attention consistency score is a sensible training-free mechanism for filtering spurious mask tracklets, and the ablation in Table 7 shows it is a meaningful contributor.

Consistent improvements over the strongest training-free baselines (Loc-Head, TAM) across models and datasets, especially on reasoning-intensive datasets, support the central claim that the proposed fusion generalizes better than heuristic head-selection methods.
The paper provides honest failure-case analysis (Appendix D) and reproduces/discusses limitations of Loc-Head and TAM, which improves transparency.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Contrastive object/background attention subtraction and video–frame attention fusion are natural extensions of existing training-free attention-based grounding methods (e.g., TAM, VL-SAM). The core components are largely recombinations of known techniques applied to the video reasoning setting.

The claim that DecAF achieves performance 'comparable to training-based methods' is only partially supported. On Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS it is competitive, but on ReVOS (Overall) it reaches 50.3 J&F vs. 61.3 for Veason-R1, 59.1 for VRS-HQ, and 54.9 for GLUS; on MeViS it reaches 43.5 vs. 52.2 for Veason-R1 and 51.3 for GLUS. The abstract and introduction overstate the level of parity with trained models.

Comparisons against training-based methods use different MLLM backbones (Chat-UniVi, LLaVA-Phi-3-V), so the 'comparable to training-based' claim conflates method quality with backbone quality. A more controlled comparison (e.g., same backbone, LoRA-finetuned baseline) would strengthen the evidence.

Several key hyperparameters (τ_pq, τ_trk, rollout layer, Otsu vs. mean thresholding) are tuned per dataset/model, and the ablation shows accuracy varies by several points depending on these choices. While the authors claim robustness, the optimal settings differ between Ref-D and ReasV, which weakens the 'no task-specific design' framing.

The V-Max normalization and the attention consistency score are introduced with limited theoretical justification; it is unclear why vision-max head weighting is preferable beyond empirical gains on two datasets.

Computational cost is not reported. Generating many point queries, running SAM2 propagation, and performing NMS across tracklets could be expensive; a runtime/memory analysis relative to baselines is missing, which matters for a 'practical, training-free' claim.

The method relies on prompt templates (object-focused, background-focused, category-choice) whose sensitivity is not systematically evaluated; prompt brittleness is a known issue for attention-based grounding and is not fully characterized.

strengths: Proposes a training-free pipeline for video reasoning segmentation that avoids fine-tuning MLLMs and SAM, using attention rollout plus SAM2 prompting.
Combines contrastive object-background fusion and complementary video-frame fusion to suppress noise and improve localization, with reasonable ablations over components.
Evaluates across multiple MLLM backbones (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL, Qwen2.5VL) and five VOS datasets, reporting both attention masks and SAM masks.
Shows consistent gains over prior training-free methods (Loc-Head, TAM) on several benchmarks, especially ReasonVOS with Qwen2.5VL, and includes threshold/scoring ablations.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'performance comparable to training-based methods' is overclaimed and not supported: on ReVOS Overall DecAF (50.3) is far below Veason-R1 (61.3) and VRS-HQ (59.1); on ReVOS Reasoning it is 45.9 vs 59.0/56.1; on MeViS it is 43.5 vs 52.2/51.3. Only a few settings (Ref-DAVIS, ReasonVOS with Qwen2.5VL) are close.

Table 2 contains an arithmetic inconsistency for Loc-Head with InternVL3-8B on ReasonVOS: J&F=39.6 but J=47.0 and F=43.3, whose average is 45.15. This undermines confidence in the reported evaluation.

Baseline comparisons are questionable: Loc-Head's original SAM prompting is replaced by the authors' prompting for all comparisons, and TAM is evaluated under a different object-focused prompt/protocol, yielding very low scores (e.g., 2.5 on Ref-DAVIS). Strong training-free baselines such as open-vocabulary detector + SAM or other MLLM grounding methods are missing.

Novelty is limited: the method is largely an engineering combination of attention rollout, head weighting, simple subtraction/averaging, thresholding, and SAM2 prompting. The individual components are heuristic and incremental over prior image-domain attention-based grounding work.

Several technical details are unclear: how attention maps are extracted from multi-token generated answers, how multiple object hypotheses are combined into final per-frame masks, how category prediction errors affect contrastive fusion, and how SAM2 propagation is configured. Prompt sensitivity is not systematically studied.

The V-Max head-weighting is not well justified and could upweight visual attention sink heads; no analysis verifies that it suppresses sink-related noise. The attention consistency score is acknowledged to fail for large objects or small briefly appearing objects, but these failure modes are not addressed.

Reproducibility is limited: code is not yet released, and there are typos/inconsistencies (e.g., 'Decoupled' vs 'Decomposed', 'Relearing', text 66.3 vs table 66.2). Scalability results are non-monotonic (InternVL3 14B not better than 8B on ReVOS) and not discussed.

strengths: Proposes a training-free framework for video reasoning segmentation that avoids model-specific fine-tuning and leverages MLLM attention maps with SAM2.

Introduces decomposed attention fusion with two intuitive mechanisms: contrastive object-background fusion and complementary video-frame fusion; ablations show consistent gains across datasets and MLLM families.
Attention-guided SAM2 prompting with an attention consistency score and NMS is a principled way to filter spurious mask tracklets without training.
Extensive evaluation across three MLLM families and five VOS datasets, with ablations on fusion, rollout method, starting layer, thresholds, MLLM scaling, and qualitative results.
Outperforms prior training-free methods such as TAM and Loc-Head by substantial margins and reaches performance competitive with several training-based methods on some benchmarks.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by public MLLM/SAM2 checkpoints, detailed prompt templates, threshold settings, and a promise to release code.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core components are simple prompt-based subtraction, averaging, thresholding, attention rollout, and SAM2 prompting, rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

Comparison with training-based methods may not be fully apples-to-apples, and the claim of comparable or superior performance is overstated: DecAF notably trails GLUS, VRS-HQ, and Veason-R1 on ReVOS, especially the reasoning split.
Training-free baselines are limited to TAM and Loc-Head; other relevant training-free grounding/segmentation approaches such as VL-SAM or open-vocabulary grounding pipelines are not compared.

Several technical details are insufficiently specified for full reproducibility, including how attention maps are extracted from multi-token answers, how rollout from a middle layer is handled, exact head-weight aggregation, and how object-category predictions are aggregated.
The V-Max head-weighting normalization is heuristic and lacks theoretical or empirical justification beyond the ablation.
No efficiency analysis is provided, despite the pipeline using multiple MLLM prompts, attention rollout, SAM2 propagation, and NMS; runtime, memory, and query counts are not reported.
Ablations miss sensitivity to number of frames, input resolution, prompt template variations, and object-category prediction accuracy, even though category errors could propagate through the method.
Known failure modes such as large objects, small or briefly appearing objects, and thin structures are shown only in the appendix and are not addressed in the method or main analysis.
Minor presentation issues and typos remain, e.g., 'Relearing' in a table, inconsistent use of 'Decoupled' vs. 'Decomposed', and unclear citation labels such as 'TAM [KYN 25]'.

strengths: The paper tackles the important and challenging problem of training-free video reasoning segmentation by leveraging the inherent localization ability of MLLMs, avoiding expensive joint training with SAM.

It proposes DecAF, which combines contrastive object-background attention fusion and complementary video-frame attention fusion, and further introduces attention-guided SAM2 prompting with an attention consistency score. These components are intuitive and well-motivated.

The experimental evaluation is extensive, covering three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL/2.5VL) and five datasets (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS). The method achieves strong results, outperforming prior training-free methods and surpassing training-based methods on ReasonVOS.

The ablation studies are thorough, validating the contribution of object-background contrastive fusion, video-frame complementary fusion, multi-scale processing, V-Max rollout normalization, layer selection, threshold choices, and the attention consistency score.

The paper provides qualitative results, failure case analysis, prompt robustness analysis, and additional analyses on part-level segmentation, multi-object scenarios, and native grounding baselines, which strengthen the empirical claims.
The method is simple and does not require model-specific training, making it potentially generalizable to other MLLMs and modalities.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental: attention rollout, contrastive prompting, multi-scale attention fusion, and SAM2 prompting are existing ideas, and the main contribution is their combination with a few heuristics (e.g., V-Max head weighting, attention consistency score). There is limited theoretical grounding for why these particular fusion mechanisms work.

Several design choices are heuristic and ad hoc, such as the V-Max normalization, the choice of starting rollout layer (middle layer), and the fixed thresholds. Performance varies substantially across MLLMs and datasets, indicating limited robustness. For example, DecAF with InternVL3-8B underperforms Loc-Head on Ref-DAVIS, and LLaVA-OV results are much lower than Qwen2.5VL.

The comparison with Loc-Head may not be entirely fair because the authors replace Loc-Head's SAM prompting with their own pipeline and adapt heuristics per model. While they justify this as isolating attention quality, it deviates from the original method and may not reflect the true performance of the baseline.

The method requires multiple MLLM forward passes (object/background prompts for both video and frame inputs) plus SAM2 propagation, which may incur high computational cost. No runtime or memory analysis is provided.

The paper claims support for multi-object segmentation, but the evaluation is primarily on single-object VOS benchmarks, and the final selection/thresholding for multiple object hypotheses is not rigorously specified or quantified.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not mention code release, and some implementation details (e.g., how point queries from all frames are fed to SAM2, exact NMS procedure, final tracklet selection for multi-object) are vague.

The claim of outperforming training-based methods is limited to ReasonVOS; on other datasets training-based methods still lead (e.g., MeViS, Ref-DAVIS). The abstract is appropriately cautious, but some statements in the introduction and conclusion may overstate the overall superiority.

strengths: The paper proposes a training-free pipeline for video reasoning segmentation that combines MLLM attention maps with SAM2, avoiding any fine-tuning.
The two proposed fusion mechanisms (contrastive object-background and complementary video-frame) are intuitive and supported by ablations showing consistent gains.

Experiments span multiple MLLM families and five datasets, including reasoning VOS, and the method achieves notably strong results on ReasonVOS, even outperforming some training-based methods with the same MLLM backbone.
The attention-guided SAM2 prompting with an attention consistency score is a reasonable idea, and the appendix provides useful analyses such as prompt robustness and native grounding baselines.
Qualitative results and failure-case analyses help illustrate the behavior of the method.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core components are heuristic combinations of existing ideas (attention rollout, contrastive prompting, simple averaging of video/frame attention, and SAM2 prompting), with little theoretical or conceptual advance.

Baseline comparisons are questionable: TAM is evaluated under an incompatible prompting scheme and reported at near-zero performance; Loc-Head's original SAM prompting is replaced with the authors' prompting; and Loc-Head is adapted with dataset- and model-specific heuristics, making the comparison unfair.

The central claim that the method achieves performance comparable to training-based methods is overstated. It is not comparable on ReVOS, MeViS, or Ref-YouTube-VOS, and the paper selectively emphasizes the one benchmark (ReasonVOS) where it is strong.

The method critically depends on object-category prediction and prompt engineering, but there is no quantitative evaluation of category prediction accuracy or analysis of how errors propagate through the pipeline.

The attention consistency score in Eq. 8 is ad hoc, not normalized to [0,1], yet it is averaged with other scores; the thresholding and penalty terms lack principled justification and appear tuned to datasets.

Attention masks alone are very weak (around 20% J&F), so most of the final dense-mask performance comes from SAM2. The contribution of the attention fusion to the final segmentation quality is therefore limited.
An important simple baseline—native Qwen2.5-VL grounding combined with SAM2—is only in the appendix, not in the main paper, which weakens the main experimental comparison.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and the method involves many hyperparameters, thresholds, and prompt choices that may be sensitive in practice.
The manuscript contains writing and reference issues (e.g., typos, inconsistent naming, garbled references), which reduce clarity and professionalism.

strengths: Introduces a training-free framework for video reasoning segmentation that leverages MLLM attention and SAM2, achieving strong results without any fine-tuning.

Proposes effective attention refinement techniques: contrastive object-background fusion to suppress visual attention sinks, complementary video-frame fusion for temporal and spatial cues, and vision-aware normalization for attention rollout.
Develops an attention-guided SAM2 prompting pipeline with point query generation, NMS, and an attention consistency score to filter spurious masks.

Extensive evaluation on five datasets (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS) and three MLLM families, with thorough ablations on fusion strategies, rollout methods, thresholds, and prompt robustness.

Demonstrates that a training-free method can outperform training-based methods on ReasonVOS and achieve comparable performance on other benchmarks, with detailed analysis of failure cases and additional scenarios (multi-object, part-level, non-explicit).
Good reproducibility: uses public checkpoints, fixed hyperparameters, and provides prompts and implementation details.
weaknesses: The claimed 'comparable to training-based methods on both referring and reasoning VOS' is slightly overstated: on ReVOS (especially the reasoning split), the method lags behind recent training-based approaches (e.g., VRS-HQ, Veason-R1) by a notable margin.

The method combines several existing ideas (attention rollout, contrastive prompting, multi-scale fusion, SAM2 prompting); the core novelty may be viewed as incremental, though the specific integration is effective.

The pipeline involves multiple MLLM forward passes and several heuristic thresholds; while ablations show robustness, the computational cost and inference time are not reported, and the complexity may hinder practical deployment.

The object category choice prompt and background exclusion rely on the MLLM correctly identifying a single object category; performance on highly ambiguous or open-vocabulary expressions could degrade, though some non-explicit cases are shown.
The attention consistency score is a heuristic with manually designed penalty terms; a more principled formulation could be explored.
